prime.problem: You've built a tokenizer, but a real model ships with someone else's. If you can't read OpenAI's files, you can't reproduce GPT-2's ids, and a model fed the wrong ids is fed nonsense. And a tokenizer made only of merges has no way to say "this document ended", because any marker spelled in text can also appear in ordinary text.
prime.fits: This is where the from-scratch tokenizer meets the real one. It reuses your vocab, merges and encode loop from the encode card and the regex split from the previous card, then adds the one thing BPE can't give you: ids reserved for control.
expect: model surgery to add a token
prime.goal: Map every part of OpenAI's encoder.py onto the tokenizer you wrote, explain why special tokens sit outside BPE, and predict what tiktoken does with a special string in user text.

attend: Which line of bpe() does the same job as the min over merge indices in your encode?
Why is the letter a id 64 in GPT-2 rather than its byte value 97, and does that change which merges happen?
Why can no amount of BPE on ordinary text ever produce id 50256?
Why does tiktoken raise an error on <|endoftext|> in text by default instead of quietly encoding it?
When you add a new special token to a trained model, which weights must change and which can stay exactly as they were?

must: encoder.json is the vocab (inverted) and vocab.bpe is the merge list in rank order, with merge #r → id 256 + r → bpe()'s min-rank loop is our encode → load the two files and you reproduce GPT-2's ids exactly (300 tokens on the Colab string)
Merges only ever create ids 256–50255 → 50256 lies outside anything BPE can reach → only code can insert <|endoftext|> → the model gets a document boundary that ordinary text can't fake

If encode parsed special strings in any input → a user could type <|endoftext|> and inject a real boundary → so tiktoken raises by default and you opt in with allowed_special (or encode it as 7 plain tokens with disallowed_special=())
New special token → new id past the end → the embedding table and lm_head each grow one row → old rows and old logits stay unchanged → only the new row gets gradient, so you can train just that row
elevated: The 256 byte tokens are numbered in byte_encoder order (printable bytes first) → a = 64, space = 220, byte 0 = 188 → a from-scratch tokenizer must remap bytes before its ids match GPT-2 or GPT-4 (the byte_shuffle in the GPT-4 exercise)
cl100k's n_vocab is 100,277 but only 100,256 BPE ids + 5 specials exist → 16 ids are unused → sizing a model by n_vocab includes rows no text ever selects
reference: the download URLs for encoder.json and vocab.bpe, and the #version: 0.2 header line that [1:-1] skips
cl100k special ids: endoftext 100257, fim_prefix/middle/suffix 100258–100260, endofprompt 100276
tiktoken's allowed_special='all' / disallowed_special=() arguments and the private _special_tokens dict

compress.prompt: Card closed: in 3–5 sentences, explain how OpenAI's two GPT-2 files correspond to what you built, and why <|endoftext|> is a separate id rather than a string. Or draw the path of '<|endoftext|>hello world' through encode twice: once as plain text, once with specials allowed.
checklist: encoder.json = vocab (string → id), vocab.bpe = merges in training order; merge rank r gives id 256 + r
bpe() repeatedly merges the lowest-rank pair, the same loop as our encode
the special id is outside the merge range, so only code can insert it; it marks document boundaries
tiktoken refuses special strings in text by default because otherwise users could inject them
the byte_encoder layer is cosmetic, except that it sets the byte ids' order

retrieve.q: Explain what a special token is, and why it has to live outside the BPE merges rather than being a very common merge.
answer: an id with a meaning set by the training setup (document boundary, FIM sentinel, chat turn), inserted by code
a merge can be produced from ordinary text, so a merged token could appear by accident or be typed by a user
an id outside the merge range can only come from your code, so it's unambiguous

retrieve.q: Walk ' world' through OpenAI's encode(): what does each of the regex, byte_encoder, bpe() and encoder.json steps turn it into?
answer: regex: ' world' stays one chunk (space + letters)
byte_encoder: its bytes become characters, so the space becomes Ġ: 'Ġworld'
bpe(): merges lowest-rank pairs until none apply, ending with the single symbol 'Ġworld'
encoder.json: 'Ġworld' → 995

retrieve.q: You're building a chat app on GPT-2's tokenizer and user messages are pasted straight into the prompt. Choose between allowed_special='all', disallowed_special=() and the default for user text, and say what each costs.
answer: 'all' on user text lets anyone inject 50256 and end the document mid-prompt: unsafe
disallowed_special=() encodes the marker as 7 plain tokens: safe, and the model sees harmless text
the default raises: safe but crashes on any message that contains the string, so you must catch it
use allowed_special only for text your own code wrote

retrieve.q: GPT-2's vocab is 50,257 and cl100k's n_vocab is 100,277. Break each number into its parts.
answer: GPT-2: 256 bytes + 50,000 merges + 1 special
cl100k: 100,256 BPE ids (256 bytes + 100,000 merges) + 5 specials + 16 unused ids

compare.q: Your encode vs OpenAI's bpe(): what is the same algorithm, what representation choice differs, and could the difference ever change the output ids?
answer: same: repeatedly pick the pair with the lowest merge rank and merge it, stop when no pair is in the table
different: ours works on integer ids, theirs on strings of byte_encoder characters joined with spaces
the ids come out identical once the bytes are mapped through GPT-2's byte order (checked: 300 tokens on the Colab string)
theirs also caches each chunk's result, which only changes speed

compare.q: GPT-2 puts its only special token at the end of the vocab (50256); sentencepiece puts <unk>, <s>, </s> at the start (0, 1, 2). What does each choice cost?
answer: end: byte and merge ids stay clean (byte tokens are 0–255), and adding a special is just appending
start: every byte token is shifted (byte id = byte + 3), a classic off-by-offset trap
both keep specials out of the merge process; only the numbering differs

compare.q: To match tiktoken, minbpe's GPT4Tokenizer needs byte_shuffle and special-token registration. Which of those follow from this card, and why?
answer: byte_shuffle: the byte tokens are numbered in byte_encoder order, so raw byte b isn't id b (a → 64)
specials: <|endoftext|> 100257, FIM and endofprompt must be registered by hand because no merge produces them

predict.q: You append <|im_start|> to GPT-2 as id 50257 with a small random embedding row and don't train yet. For the prompt 'hello world', do the logits of the old 50,257 tokens change? Do their probabilities change?
predict.answer: The old logits are identical (the lab measures old logits unchanged: True): the old rows of lm_head didn't change and the input ids don't use the new row. The probabilities do change slightly, because softmax divides by a sum that now includes one more term, exp(new logit), so every old probability shrinks a little. Until you fine-tune, the new token gets a small, arbitrary share of probability.

apply.task: Load encoder.json and vocab.bpe into your tokenizer instead of OpenAI's code. Build shuffle = {b: encoder[byte_encoder[b]]} for the 256 bytes and merges = {(encoder[a], encoder[b]): encoder[a+b]} for all 50,000 lines. Then run your encode on each GPT-2 regex chunk of the Colab example string (map bytes through shuffle first) and compare with tiktoken.get_encoding('gpt2'). Then skip the regex split and encode the whole string at once.
apply.done: With the regex split you get exactly 300 ids, equal to tiktoken's list; without it you get 296. You should be able to explain why skipping the split changes the count (merges then cross category boundaries).
apply.hint: Import bytes_to_unicode from encoder.py for byte_encoder. Every merge maps to id 256 + its rank, so the min over merges.get in your encode already picks the lowest rank.
